questions.learningObjective: State what an alpha level commits the author to

options.misconception: Believes a preregistered alpha fixes the required sample size

options.text: Publishing every outcome of the study, including the null results

Accepting any additional analysis that reuses the same star catalogue

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish exploratory from confirmatory analysis
questions.stem: Explain to a visiting club member the difference between exploratory and confirmatory analysis in a sky survey you run yourself.

answer.exemplar: Exploratory analysis searches the data for patterns, so its questions are chosen after looking at the data and its results are hypothesis-generating. Confirmatory analysis tests a question fixed in advance against data not used to choose that question, so a significant result supports the original claim.

questions.explanation: The distinction turns on when the question was fixed relative to looking at the data. Calling an analysis confirmatory only because it produced a small p-value reverses the logic of the distinction.
questions.hint: Ask when the question was decided.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A confirmatory test on data already examined
questions.learningObjective: Compute the family-wise error rate from repeated tests
questions.stem: You tested 20 candidate variable stars at alpha 0.05 each after inspecting their light curves. Treating these as independent tests, what family-wise error rate does 1 - 0.95^20 give, as a proportion?
questions.explanation: Each test carries a 0.05 chance of a false positive, so at least one across 20 tests has probability 1 - 0.95^20 = 0.6415. Testing after looking at the data makes that inflation real.
questions.hint: Compute 0.95 to the twentieth power.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A confirmatory test on data already examined
questions.learningObjective: Explain why earlier inspection weakens a confirmatory claim
questions.stem: Explain why running a preregistered statistical test on data I have already inspected does not produce a confirmatory result.

answer.exemplar: The confirmatory label depends on the question being fixed before the data were used to shape it. Once I have looked at the data, I know which patterns the data can produce, so any test I run afterwards, even one that was preregistered, is chosen with that knowledge and its error rate is inflated.

questions.explanation: Pre-registering a test fixes its form but does not un-see the data. Once inspection has occurred, the same test carries the analyst's accumulated knowledge, so claims must be softened to exploratory.
questions.hint: A written plan cannot undo earlier looking.

questions.stem: Explain to a co-author why I should not report a confirmatory claim from the same star sample I used while exploring.

answer.exemplar: Exploration and confirmation have to use separate evidence, because exploration tells me which patterns the sample can produce and I then choose a question that fits what I saw. questions.learningObjective: Explain what a preregistration protects against

answer.exemplar: The preregistration records the decisions I fixed before seeing the data: which analysis, which exclusions, what counts as a finding. questions.learningObjective: Interpret an unstated rule in a preregistration
questions.stem: My preregistration fixes the sample size, the test and the alpha, but leaves the outlier rule unstated. What does this mean for how my results are read?

options.text: The outlier rule was mine to choose, so readers should be told which rule I used and when it was set
The preregistration is invalid, because every possible analysis detail must be fixed in advance
options.misconception: Believes preregistration must fix every possible detail

options.text: The results are unconstrained, since any unplanned detail makes every test exploratory
options.misconception: Believes any unspecified rule makes every test exploratory

options.text: Nothing, because the preregistration covers only the sample size and the alpha level
options.misconception: Believes preregistration covers only sample size and alpha

questions.explanation: An unspecified detail is a gap rather than a fatal flaw, and the remedy is disclosure: state the rule used and whether it was fixed before or after seeing the data. Blanket invalidity is an overstatement.
questions.hint: An unstated rule must be declared, not ignored.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to label analyses honestly
questions.stem: Explain to a visiting student how I can label the analyses in my astronomy club study honestly without overstating them.

answer.exemplar: I name each analysis by when its question was fixed relative to seeing the data. Anything prompted by looking at the data is labelled exploratory, with the reason it was added, and only questions registered in advance are called confirmatory. I state that the confirmatory claims rest on the registered plan and that the exploratory findings are offered as hints for future work.

questions.explanation: Honest labelling turns on dates and reasoning rather than how exciting a result looks. Splitting the two kinds of work lets a reader weigh the confirmatory claims without being misled by the exploratory ones.
questions.hint: Label by when the question was fixed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A confirmatory test on data already examined
questions.learningObjective: Compute a per-test alpha under a Bonferroni adjustment
questions.stem: I ran 24 candidate significance tests on the same variable stars and wanted a family-wise rate of 0.05. Under a Bonferroni adjustment, what per-test alpha value did I use?
questions.explanation: Bonferroni divides the family-wise threshold by the number of tests, so 0.05 over 24 gives 0.002083. It keeps the overall false positive rate at 0.05 even though the analyst has already looked at the data.
questions.hint: Divide 0.05 by the number of tests.
